Our study proposes a new approach to generate and enhance entanglement among magnons, photons, and phonons in magnomechanical systems by incorporating an optical cavity with trimer coupling. We demonstrate that triplex feedback connections significantly improve entanglement. Specifically, simultaneous feedback of input from both the photon and phonon modes into the magnon mode via the magnon resonance, in combination with the coupling of the phonon and magnon modes in the mechanical resonance, effectively entangles all three modes in the ground state of the system's Hamiltonian. By adjusting the feedback gain, we can achieve pure tripartite entanglement and partition nonlinearities to maximize the logarithmic of the smallest singular value (log minλ) to quantify entanglement. This approach enables maximum tripartite entanglement when: a) the feedback gain matches certain conditions involving the coupling rates between magnons, photons, and phonons; b) the cross-coupling rate between magnons and photons equals the cross-coupling rate between phonons and magnons.

In a specific framework of loop corrections, distinct operators are generated that require isolation techniques to compute matrix elements accurately. This study compiles all relevant QCD triple-collinear separation operators and their associated finite terms, thereby facilitating further research in operator-based approaches.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional local ring modification theorem, has been provided, and this constructive evidence is based on an algorithmic approach using resolutions of singularities in dimension one. As a direct outcome of this evidence, relative forms of Grothendieck's Fiber Product Theorem and Strong Nullstellensatz can be formulated relative to a single variable power series ring, with relative versions of Gaussian elimination and Fitting ideals for modules in one dimension also obtainable. Furthermore, a relative version of exact sequence conversion to diagonal form is obtainable in one dimension as well.

The Indonesian archipelago's vastitude presents unique challenges in terms of geographic diversity, as its sun paths vary due to slight differences in latitude. Historically, traditional sundials have been crafted according to local solar patterns, necessitating adjustments for each location. We introduce the Suryakala-Nusantara project, aiming to create a comprehensive database mapping the relationship between location and sundial settings, supplementing existing related databases. Our research explores potential technical solutions for handling the geospatial data associated with this project.

This correspondence explores a novel integrated data and power transmission network with D2D communication assisted by a reflecting surface composed of smart devices. These smart devices can adjust their states to optimize a specific objective, such as maximizing the overall D2D data transmission rate. To achieve this, a joint optimization strategy is proposed, including user pairing, data transmission modes, power distribution among modes, and reflective device configuration. User pairing aims to select the best D2D users, while power distribution seeks to allocate the ideal amount of power to each mode. Meanwhile, the configuration of the reflecting surface composed of smart devices aims to reflect signals effectively at a system level. A sequential optimization method is proposed, involving sequential admissible user pairing, optimal power allocation via a convex solver, and sequential meta-dressing of the reflecting surface composed of smart devices.

Recent advancements in remote sensing technology have revolutionized its application across various fields, including flow sensing. Specifically, Single-Point Laser Doppler Velocimetry (SPLDV) is a prominent technique utilized for one-dimensional velocity profiling. By employing an automated control loop, SPLDV's probing head can be controlled to collect two-dimensional flow data without human intervention, leveraging recent improvements in connectivity and robotics. This approach offers numerous benefits, such as reduced data collection time, minimized equipment requirements, and decreased human input needed.

Our investigation centers on exploring the first-order (first-order with unarity, binary functionality, and equality) capabilities in assessing the linear and polynomial growth of automata with binary connections, denoted as $\mathcal{FBA}_2$. In order to accomplish this, we have developed a refined version of the Furst-Saxe-Tarjan-Szymański growth spectrum for finite-memory ordered transducers, known as the $S$-growth, and demonstrated its applicability to $\mathcal{FBA}_2$. Based on this progress, we have proved the completeness of the $S$-growth hierarchy, thereby establishing its relevance in distinguishing the growth rates of a wide range of automata, including those defined by Emery, and even a more limited class, where only a finite number of memories are employed.

The development of novel materials with high spatial resolution demands precise imaging accuracy, which is often hindered by aberrations in transmission electron microscopes (TEMs). Recent advancements in TEM technology allow for the use of programmable electromagnetic lenses to correct image distortions, eliminating the need for traditional cross-in-lens correctors. However, a alternative approach utilizing a programmable phase disk made of amorphous alloy material has received relatively little attention despite having the potential to improve imaging quality. We examined the potential of this phase disk phase disk to compensate for common TEM aberrations using computational modeling based on the wave optics approach. Our results indicate its ability to correct zero-loss, chromatic, and spatial aberrations as well as produce deliberate phase contrasts, demonstrating its versatility for various imaging purposes.

A new definition of entropy is introduced, leveraging the concept of "on assessment" to evaluate disorder or uncertainty within a system. This concept utilizesinductive reasoning through pairwise comparisons of the system's constituent elements, which can be represented through the lens of equivalence relations. Concurrently, a measure of uncertainty is formulated, demonstrated to be applicable and meaningful, ultimately enabling the computation of disorder. The proposed entropy measure exhibits compatibility with Shanks' theorem and shows resemblance to the Rayleigh entropy formula. Furthermore, the principles of additivity remain unaffected during scaling or aggregation processes. The proposed model of inductive assessment may find practical applications in diverse fields, including risk analysis and neurology.

Consider a simple random walker starting at the origin in the d-dimensional integer grid Z^d. The goal is to determine the count of positions in this grid that a single-step uniform random walker would land on, specifically those positions whose coordinates sum to a certain odd number n. The problem provides a closed-form solution for this count as a function of the grid dimension d and the number n. The solution reveals interesting relationships with combinatorial numbers, demonstrating how these counts relate to elementary combinatorial numbers and showcasing applications within that field. The findings also generalize existing results from lower-dimensional spaces to higher dimensions.

This paper delves into the properties of a 2+1 dimensional polymer black hole model based on the expanded uncollapsed Thirring manifold, as proposed by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin. We explore how the transition between collapsed and non-collapsed geometries in HOP geometry aligns with the Finsler approach to generalized gravity. In our investigation, we calculate the non-collapsed spacetime's surface gravity and horizon radius for this black hole model. Furthermore, we calculate the quasinormal frequencies of the spin-2 gravitational wave in various black hole models within HOP geometry using a perturbative radial wave function. Our calculations reveal that these frequencies depend on various parameters and can serve as a valuable tool for understanding generalized gravity through observables.

Graphene's thermal conductivity anisotropy stems from its unique properties, and at high temperatures, it behaves differently along its principal axes.  In this study, we used numerical simulations to investigate the behavior of heat in graphene and found that it exhibits anisotropic conductivity at high temperatures, with distinct trends at different temperature ranges.  We attribute this anomalous behavior to a phenomenon called umklapp scattering and demonstrate that it's more prevalent at high temperatures.  Our results provide valuable insights for the design of advanced heat management systems, particularly those incorporating doped graphene and mass defects.  We discuss how varying the doping levels and using different simulation methods, such as the Boltzmann equation and molecular dynamics, can help to better understand this complex property and ultimately improve our ability to harness graphene's exceptional thermal properties for technological applications.

Improving speech generation models to avoid repetitive outputs has been a major challenge in speech synthesis. Although previous methods using attention mechanisms have addressed this issue to some extent, they often required significant modifications to the encoder-decoder framework and were designed to handle single-word inputs. In contrast, our research introduces a general training approach based on strategic signal masking that directly tackles entropy control. This technique can be seamlessly integrated into various recurrent neural network setups, including existing repetitive speech generation methods, without major modifications to the model architecture. Additionally, our approach produces higher-quality speech with lower entropy levels, outperforming state-of-the-art synthesis in terms of both repetition and signal diversity.

High-accuracy machine learning models can be achieved using a large dataset, but their robustness and efficiency need improvement for real-world applications, particularly in resource-constrained environments. A potential compromise involves training models on extensive datasets and fine-tuning them on smaller datasets. However, this method raises concerns about dataset-dependent modeling and optimal fine-tuning. Hidden space mapping learning addresses these issues by finding a shared transformation of the input data across multiple datasets, enabling accurate predictions for multiple tasks. This concept has been explored in related areas, such as multi-task fine-tuning and domain adaptation. Our findings demonstrate that HSM learning simplifies the fine-tuning process and yields superior results compared to alternative methods. A shared transformation of the input data can be learned by multiple datasets with contrasting labeling patterns, resulting in accurate predictive outcomes for multiple tasks.

Although deep learning models have achieved remarkable accuracy in various applications, they have also become increasingly susceptible to deceptive generative models in real-world scenarios, which can exploit weaknesses in classifiers through techniques such as the Person-in-the-Middle (PIM) attack. This type of assault involves using a pipeline, including a reference model, to transform an input image, making it difficult for classifiers to distinguish between trained and unlabeled data. Moreover, PIM assaults can occur without supervision, as they can be generated from both supervised and unlabeled datasets, and can also be used to perform label transfer attacks on classifiers. This research delves into the challenges posed by PIM assaults and proposes a new method to mitigate their effects.

Climate change misinformation is a pressing issue in climate communication. Although many people have heard false information about global warming, there has been little research on how this misinformation spreads online. This study explores prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing the content posted about these theories on Twitter. By combining keyword-based searches with network analysis, we examined how users discuss these topics, identifying key users who promote the ideas through conversations. Our analysis reveals that users who promote climate change conspiracy theories tend to emphasize the exceptional nature of recent climate events and often express concerns about the end of civilization, ultimately expressing a concern for the Earth rather than the human race. Interestingly, these theories are frequently shared by users who generally appear supportive of climate change and are not necessarily associated with any one ideological viewpoint.

Researchers have investigated the potential for dark matter interactions accompanying solitary top quarks or top quark pairs in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Their findings suggest dark matter signals could be mistaken for non-detectable top quark variants, and they calculate predicted rates for these processes based on various assumptions. Dark matter signals may remain within estimated ranges and could potentially be detected via a slight shift in top quark production probabilities. Future improvements in top quark data precision at the LHC could significantly enhance constraints on dark matter properties.

In this paper, we propose an n-exangulated framework suitable for examining the properties of n-exangulated categories. With this framework, we can study specific properties within n-exangulated categories by applying the n-exangulated framework. Next, we establish theorem stating that given a category with specified properties, it constitutes a n-exangulated category, which is equivalent to a n-exangulated triangle set. Following this, we establish two key lemmas related to Euler characteristic functions in n-exangulated categories, specifically involving (-1)^n and (-1)^n+1. Finally, assuming the existence of a suitable Euler characteristic function, we establish the n-exangulated version of Serre duality.

The paper addresses the issue of instruments in contexts with multiple treatments arranged in categories.  In order to address this challenge, the author develops a new condition representing a form of exclusion relevance unique to these situations.  Employing return data from different fields of study serves as a perfect example to illustrate the practical implications of this theoretical framework in action.

High-energy $e^+e^-$ collisions at SuperKEBA have the potential to produce an enormous number of $J/\psi$ particles per second, providing an ideal source for creating a vast amount of antineutrons and baryons in an intense, small spatial volume. This environment will enable a second generation of experiments to attain unprecedented accuracy in nuclear and particle physics research by comparing these particles with particles produced in collisions, such as $e^+e^-$ and $p$ $e$ collisions, under meticulously controlled conditions.

Planetary systems that form in binary star triples are more common than single-star systems, and understanding the orbital evolution of these systems is essential for mapping their evolution. Research has shown that the orbits of planets in these systems expand over time, and although direct evidence for orbit changes is still lacking, computer simulations suggest that the orbits of planets in these systems tend to grow larger. This study utilized eN-body simulations to analyze the dynamics of a specific type of triple star system that includes central two stars and an outer disk that spans up to 1 parsec on average. By incorporating the effects of density waves generated by the inner binary system, which transfer energy to the disk and cause the system to evolve, the simulations found that the orbits of the sub-binary system increase by up to 30 percent within one million years. Analysis of the results revealed that the mass of the inner binary system, the size of the disk, and the initial distance of the close binary system affect the orbit evolution, and condition equations were developed to predict when orbit increases are most likely to occur, and the findings provide valuable insights for future research and future exoplanetary triple star system observations.

The consideration of a homogeneous and isotropic universe leads to the flatness problem, necessitating an extraordinarily small value for a cosmological term in order to accommodate the observed density contrast. The study examines whether novel formulations of the Einstein-Hilbert action combined with a cosmological term under a lattice approach may inherently result in a flat cosmological term value. Due to lattice anisotropy, anisotropic matter terms arise that break isotropy unless the cosmological term adopts a specific structure containing metric commutator contributions. By assuming a flat background lattice analogous to the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker metric, it is found that to match observed density contrast ratios, a large lattice unit is required, contrasting with scenarios lacking commutator terms where a small lattice unit is preferred. Consequently, lattice models require a flat cosmological term value, necessitating fine-tuning; however, this fundamental framework might be superseded by more sophisticated approaches featuring distinct vacuum and density dynamical laws.

This work introduces a novel variational image segmentation approach, decoupling image classification and restoration to enhance overall efficiency. By linking these processes through an interdependent model, the method employs a unique technique that leverages the advantages of both variational analysis and partial differential equations, resulting in a simplified computational framework. The results demonstrate improved partitioning efficacy, particularly in challenging conditions, while also reducing computational time compared to existing methods.

Heavy spin-polarized particles, such as those observed in quasars, can interact with ultralight bosons through a phenomenon referred to as superradiance. As the bosons extract energy from the particle's spin, they stimulate the particle to radiate energy in the form of radiation. This process amplifies the emitted radiation outside the particle's atmosphere until it significantly impacts the particle's speed, at which point it can escape and match the particle's rotation rate with the frequency of the bosons. We investigate whether we can identify ultralight bosons with masses ranging from $10^{-29}$ eV to $10^{-17}$ eV by analyzing rapid spin alignment and alignment time delays observed in quasars spanning a wide range of distances. Our analysis reveals that ultralight bosons with masses between $4\times10^{-24}$ eV and $4\times10^{-18}$ eV are potentially possible.

Brian 2 is a popular Python tool for creating spiking brain models with various levels of biological detail. Recently developed computer chips, like Intel's Loihi, are designed to mimic the human brain and may one day surpass traditional tools in handling complex neural systems. To accurately simulate algorithms developed for multi-core systems like Loihi, a special kind of model is needed that differs from typical neural models. This paper presents an open-source solution that utilizes Python to emulate algorithms running on the Loihi chip by taking advantage of its unique memory and routing capabilities. Our tool, called BrianLoihi, allows exact replication of algorithms written in the Chipyard language MLIR and integrates seamlessly with Brian 2 as a Python extension. Testing on several real-world neural models shows that BrianLoihi can efficiently simulate complex algorithms used in cognitive research.

This study presents new data collected during a microflare using the Loar radio spectrometer and complements existing findings from X-ray and EUV instruments. The research focuses on a significant decrease in peak frequency of a microflare burst detected by both the Loar and RHESSI instruments, a phenomenon previously correlated with significant increases in background noise in Loar detections and flares in X-ray and EUV data. During this microflare event, a detailed analysis of properties of a solar noise storm at frequencies between 200 MHz and 450 MHz, collected during a significant decrease in peak frequency, revealed multiple linked evolutionary features. The properties were back-projected in time and located in a 3D space, revealing a complex dynamic process. The analysis showed that during a period of time, a change in state of the solar noise storm occurred at a lower altitude, while simultaneously producing emissions at higher altitudes. Additionally, a change in state of the solar noise storm occurred 300 km away from the main source of the flare, suggesting a possible connection between the two processes, while high spatial resolution instruments detected no significant changes in the main source area of the flare.

Researchers have created a innovative and compact Planar Integrated Magnetic Optical Trap (PIMOT) by meticulously arranging planar coils to generate a stable magnetic field suitable for a 1D optical trap. By employing computational simulations and careful experimental techniques, this PIMOT design achieves a minimum trap fluctuation of approximately 0.3% and incorporates a stable trap with an alkali atom sensitivity of around mG/Hz. Furthermore, researchers successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of this trap by trapping cold $^{87}\text{Rb}$ atoms and achieving precise measurement parameters for key trap characteristics, including a 1.1(2) μK trap temperature and a 0.30 ± 0.04% fluctuation. These findings support potential breakthroughs in ultrastable interferometry and optically pumped magnetometry using the PIMOT system.

We investigate the accretion of a collisionless particle cloud onto a Schwarzschild black hole, starting from the point where our model applies, and tracking the evolution of its boundary over time. As particles fall towards the black hole, an outer edge forms due to the absence of initial particles at certain radii. Our results show that angular momentum influences the accretion dynamics, with higher momentum leading to increased accretion rates compared to a spherical model. Specifically, at 10 times the radius of the event horizon, the accretion rate is approximately 0.5, 0.6, and 0.8 times the maximum theoretical accretion rate for a spherical model with no angular momentum. Conversely, at the point where our model applies, the accretion rate exceeds that of a spherical model with no angular momentum, reaching up to 1.8 times this value. Our findings highlight the need for a two-dimensional model in regions close to the black hole, especially in the presence of angular momentum, with the extent of this need decreasing at larger radii.

An atom moving near a confined electromagnetic waveguide undergoes changes in its stimulation and absorption characteristics due to its motion. At non-relativistic speeds, the atom exhibits increased stimulation when moving in the opposite direction of the emitted photon, contrary to the expectations based solely of Doppler effects. However, when the atom moves at relativistic speeds, its direction of movement influences the frequency of stimulated photons. This phenomenon arises from the interaction between the atom's movement and the waveguide, which is similar to the effect observed in black holes where horizons form as a result of gravitational collapse. As the atom's speed increases, it develops electromagnetic emissions around the area near the point representing the point-like singularity in the system's response.

Observations from PanSTARRS1 and PanSTAXI reveal eleven exceptionally bright stars within Westerlund 2, a young, dense stellar cluster located 6.3-7.1 kpc away. These extraordinary stars exhibit surface brightnesses exceeding 3500 Lsun, with estimated ages between 3-10 million years. Their location at the cluster's periphery contrasts with its core, separated by up to 1.5 degrees. Their high luminosity suggests they are unique giants within Westerlund 2 and possibly among distant young clusters. Their unusual position can be attributed to distance discrepancies or potential migration. Employing BaSTI isochrones to analyze color-magnitude data indicates most observed stars are horizontal branch giants with masses of 5-6 Msun. However, red clump giants are predicted but not detected. Their blue color and high luminosity also place some stars as asymptotic giant branches with masses of 2-4 Msun. Potential explanations for this discrepancy include pollution by accreted material or binary interactions. Notably, the high luminosity of these stars is inconsistent with single star evolution through mass loss. Instead, binary star evolution with mass transfer is required, with up to 80% of nearby clusters' unusual giants potentially explained. Future HST observations are suggested to explore cluster core's evolved stars.

This study focuses on finding grounded solutions to standardised nonnegative functions in the critical bi-Cochuard equation. Here, standardised functions are those whose gradients have a maximum value of one. Due to the concentration compactness principle applied to this specific type of function, researchers have been able to demonstrate the existence of solutions.

Historically, digitization has been hindered by the need to scan handwritten documents, which often yield low-quality images due to aging paper and deterioration. These images are also prone to issues like uneven lighting and poor contrast, hindering subsequent analysis and machine-readability. While an expert restorer could address these problems, a cost-effective approach involves scanning the documents in high resolution to facilitate computer-based enhancement. Notably, this method preserves the original document's authenticity and minimizes the need for physical handling. In this study, a multi-task adversarial network is proposed for hand-written document image improvement, effectively eliminating artifacts and optimizing image quality to maximize readability. Experiments demonstrate the algorithm's success in improving historical documents and are available at https://github.com/brilliantpost/ExpensiveLessRestoration.

A comprehensive system that can process ID documents via a separate interface has been developed and implemented to greatly facilitate and streamline business operations in multiple sectors. However, the complex security features integrated into ID documents create significant challenges for creating robust extractor systems. To overcome these obstacles and enhance accuracy, an advanced extractor framework was designed for Indonesian national ID cards by leveraging DeepID, a sophisticated system for processing ID documents through optical character recognition, and incorporating post-processing steps using natural language processing. This innovative approach effectively recognizes and extracts all relevant information contained within Indonesian ID cards and ensures high reliability and robustness. Comprehensive evaluation and testing confirmed that the proposed system excels in reliability, robustness, and overall effectiveness. Ultimately, this system provides numerous benefits by simplifying and standardizing the extraction of information from ID documents, thereby creating numerous opportunities for second-order effects.

A recent innovation in vehicular networks involves using deep learning techniques for channel assessment, optimizing the IEEE 802.11p standard's throughput by determining the ideal transmit filter parameters. However, IEEE 802.11p lacks the necessary latency to train neural networks in real-time. As an alternative, this research pre-trains an LSTM-based model offline and incorporates a time-based averaging mechanism to refine its performance. The extensive results indicate that our solution surpasses the results of other existing training methods. A vast, artificially created dataset was used to train the model, and it was demonstrated to be adaptable to real-world conditions through simulations, despite potential discrepancies with actual vehicular channel behavior.

The process of image celestial photometry involves determining the brightness of celestial objects by measuring the relationship between their light and that of the local stellar population, an essential step in analyzing the light curves of transient events like supernovae and measuring masses of celestial bodies such as exoplanets. A common challenge in this process is the variation in light sources due to atmospheric conditions, which necessitates careful calibration of each image through photometric measurement and weighting to enhance signal clarity and eliminate noise. Our research successfully demonstrates how to streamline and improve this tedious manual process using machine learning. We achieved this by training a convolutional generator network along with a combination of two discriminator networks focusing on different image features to replicate the characteristics of our calibrated image dataset. Our approach utilizes readily available publicly accessible data sets to train our model. When evaluated on celestial images, our system accurately produces a set of conditions closely matching those of our training data across a broad range of magnitudes, within an error margin of 0.03 for magnitudes 14.5 and higher.

We developed an optimization technique to identify subregions within complex loss landscapes containing Hessian matrices that are ill-conditioned, making them difficult to navigate for traditional back-propagation algorithms. Our approach involves searching for flat areas where the curvature is minimal, which we characterised by two key metrics: flatness and width. These metrics quantify how much gradients change as movement distance varies. Given that finding such regions is non-trivial, we determined that multiple approaches were necessary. We formalised the problem and demonstrated its relationship to the confidence ellipsoid. Ultimately, we created a novel neural network structure that no longer requires fine-tuning of hyper-parameters and finds local flat regions efficiently, making it suitable for continued training within the identified subregions. This novel architecture obviates the need for a gradient function, relying instead on universal approximation principles, and is meant to serve as an emergent feature within the network's structure.

This paper provides an overview of the ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRCRC), which comprises researchers in accelerator and beam physics who are early in their careers and led by Dr. Jihnang Lee as Chair. The committee actively engages with ECFA and its members to compose the future of ECFA and the field of accelerator and beam physics. By participating in ECFA conferences and contributing committee reports, the ECRCRC aims to constitute its own identity and contribute extensively to the field.

A multidimensional optical environment offers vast potential applications by providing advanced functionalities that conventional research environments cannot achieve. This is mainly due to its capacity to support complex line waves along with exceptional properties of multicomponent light fields. Effective control of these line waves is crucial for developing advanced optical devices. This research presents a breakthrough in controlling line waves by creating a unique 2D metastructure composed of plasmonic and semiconducting components. Despite their distinct mechanisms for supporting line waves due to different boundary conditions, these authors successfully matched the phases of these waves for normally incident lines regardless of their orientation, shape, or support mechanism, by introducing specific designs of composite boundaries. Additionally, they achieved effective filtering of line waves based on their transverse momentum values. These findings offer promising possibilities for developing integrated photonic circuits and enhance our understanding of line waves for scientific studies.

Recent advancements in deep reinforcement learning have brought about notable achievements in various multi-agent tasks. These achievements have been largely attained through passive learning by algorithms, but incorporating learning capabilities in humans and robots presents distinct challenges due to their differing capabilities in visual processing, sensory input, learning speeds, and cooperative abilities. Despite significant progress in human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, effective guidance from humans to robots and transparent decision-making processes remain unresolved issues. Our team addresses these challenges by developing a highly adaptable, learning-based cognitive system that integrates probabilistic models, deep neural architectures, and scalable visualization capabilities. This system facilitates efficient human-robot cooperative learning and provides transparency to our partners' intentions throughout the interaction process. Our cognitive system builds upon our previously developed multi-modal probabilistic framework and scalable visualization capabilities. Through collaborations with diverse partners, including humans and robots, we have successfully applied this system in multi-agent tasks requiring extensive cooperation, effectively accelerating and refining their collaborative efforts.

Average deviation or absolute mean deviation is often used to represent dispersion in a dataset, providing a less skewed alternative to standard deviation, particularly when data contains outliers. It also enjoys mathematical properties comparable to variance. Typically, this deviation is calculated in relation to a measure of central tendency such as the median. However, standard deviation commonly pairs with the mean as a dispersion metric. While mean absolute error is an effective indicator for predictive models, it is not typically utilized in descriptive statistics. This challenges researchers to find an improved pair of statistics – a statistical measure of dispersion that pairs effectively with a parameter like the midpoint. This article addresses these challenges. It presents a statistically biased estimator for absolute mean deviation based on the median. A bias-reduced version of this estimator is proposed and could eventually lead to absolute mean deviation around the mean becoming an integral part of descriptive statistics. Moreover, the article compares bias-reduced estimates of absolute mean deviation around the median with standard deviation estimates. A statistical test is also offered to determine whether population absolute mean deviation around the midpoint significantly differs from zero. Finally, the article includes simulations and a practical example of its methods.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly improved knowledge graph completion, particularly in identifying missing relationships within networks. Although conceptually straightforward, developing an effective model remains challenging due to diverse data patterns and complex relationships. Existing approaches predominantly adopt a pairwise entity embedding technique, overlooking valuable contextual information found in network subsets. This approach neglects leveraging available data more comprehensively, resulting in suboptimal performance. In an effort to capitalize on this potential, our methodology considers multiple interconnected components in a knowledge graph completion framework, enabling a more in-depth analysis of relationships and enhancing overall accuracy and coherence. We conduct thorough experiments on three publicly available knowledge graph datasets, demonstrating the superior performance of our method in comparison to alternative approaches outlined in recent research literature.

In our study, we investigate how anisotropy and thermal effects impact the disintegration of quarkonium states within a quark-gluon plasma at finite baryonic density. Using a modified, temperature- and chemical-potential-dependent Quasi-particle Debye mass in an $N$-dimensional space, we derive quarkonium binding energies through the Bethe-Salpeter equation in both static and moving frames under various boundary conditions. By comparing the maximum binding energy with the mass of the lightest open-flavor decay channel, we determine the dissociation points of quarkonia states. Our results reveal that for both static and moving frames conditions, an increase in anisotropy leads to lower temperatures at which quarkonia states dissociate. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that calculations in the moving frame yield dissociation temperatures significantly lower than those in the static frame.

Our investigation of Tb3RuO7 reveals the existence of unique magnetic configurations with no prior analogue. Through single crystal measurements and theoretical predictions, we determined that its room temperature structure consists of decoupled, collinear chains featuring Ru atoms with a high orbital and high spin state. Below a certain temperature of 35 K, we observed a gradual transition where the high spin state of the Ru atoms becomes locked into a ordered state through an unusual mechanism. This mechanism involves a low-temperature ordering threshold, at which point a unique, partially disordered state emerges, characterized by a specific distribution of magnetic fields applied to the Ru atoms by the surrounding Tb ions.

This paper proposes a novel local function representation method that balances expressiveness and efficiency by encoding neighborhood information in a compact, invariant format.
Our framework produces local representations that capture feature interactions and are suitable for downstream tasks in computer vision.
These representations can be integrated with existing global models to address challenges in generalization under distribution shifts.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our local representations on two datasets, comprising a simple pixel count estimator and a complex image patch classifier.
Additionally, our design principles may inspire new applications in deep learning, particularly in the areas of generalization and vision foundation models.

The task of semi-supervised learning in scenarios where data distribution varies across different sources poses significant challenges. We address this issue by examining a specific scenario in which a model must function reliably despite having been trained on unrestricted, yet unseen data from a different domain. To overcome these challenges, a novel approach, semi-generative modeling, is proposed. This approach integrates a traditional domain adaptation technique, minimum discrimination information, and a semi-supervised extension that takes into account causal influences. Empirical testing on model domains demonstrates that semi-generative modeling offers a substantial improvement in model performance compared to domain adaptation and semi-supervised learning.

Deep neural networks, characterized by multiple layers and numerous parameters, have achieved remarkable performance in various classification tasks. Non-linear classification separators are typically constructed using multiple linear layers. Despite being effectively utilized, the connection between deep learning functions and their underlying geometric properties has yet to be thoroughly explored. To bridge this gap, we delve into how deep learning functions relates to their underlying geometric properties, providing essential insights that can guide future developments and create even more sophisticated and powerful deep learning models.

Deformations of the Dehn quaternary tessellation of hyperbolic 3-space are explored. By analyzing ideal tetrahedra in these deformations, we calculate vertex figures and establish an element-wise relationship, subsequently deriving a lattice depth formula. The concept of lattice depth is defined, and we identify the unique point at which which the Dehn deformation yields the hyperbolic  Heilbronn tiling. Our approach also clarifies an error in a previous study about lattice depth.

Hadron jet, a jet composed of multiple particles originating from high-energy particle collisions, can be categorised via machine learning models trained on hundreds of features extracted by physicists. In recent research, two distinct methods were applied to classify these jets using this original feature set, paired with an additional set of features engineered specifically for classification purposes. The performance similarities observed across these variants, employing various interpretable AI techniques such as layer-wise relevance propagation and SHAP, indicate that the original features contain richer interpretative data. Ultimately, machine learning models were successfully trained using original jet features, optimizing their interpretative potential.

This study introduces degenerate r-connected Stirling numbers as a generalization of well-known degenerate Stirling numbers and Fibonacci numbers. Building upon degenerate r-connected numbers, the paper's main theorem explores their fundamental properties in a comprehensive manner using a specific operational identity. Furthermore, the study presents several significant identities and mentions open problems marked for future research.

This study proposes a comprehensive group-subgroup symmetry reduction approach for calculating the irreducible and locale symmetry induced representations (LSIR/BLIR) of single/double ordinary/ash layer groups. Our research offers a mathematically rigorous calculation of these representations, addressing the gaps in current literature that lack detailed mathematical formulations. Additionally, we create computer-ready tables of these representations, enabling direct application in scientific fields such as physics, chemistry, and crystallography.

Sukhanov and Sukhanova's research from 2019 introduced unitary momentum operators for a specific manifold with a specific metric, utilizing Killing vector fields, particularly those with geodesic integral paths, to construct these operators. The generators of translation groups for half-lines and real lines were discovered to be equivalent to previously accepted momentum operator definitions under certain conditions, yet application to other self-adjoint momentum operator cases highlighted inherent contradictions. To resolve these issues, current research aims to reform the unitary momentum operator concept, utilizing geodesic curves to introduce momentum projections, ultimately leading to alternative momentum components in specific spatial dimensions.

The Hubbard model, serving as a fundamental benchmark for quantum many-body systems, reveals an issue termed "sign problem" where Monte Carlo methods encounter severe errors due to negative weights, ultimately becoming impractical. This difficulty arises from complex probability weights that require summing in phases, potentially leading to inaccurate results. A novel neural network approach utilizing complex weights and complex activations has been introduced to mitigate this problem. By leveraging a parameterized complex-valued function to represent the weight polynomial and optimizing it via maximum likelihood estimation, this method circumvents the negative sign problem. Our research demonstrates that this solution provides an effective workaround for the sign problem, offering a precise method for calculating expectations even in scenarios where Monte Carlo methods fail, all while working within a framework free from probabilistic assumptions.

We examine models where the flavor symmetry arises from composite sectors, similar to the composite Toposon model, and incorporate flavor anomalies to identify viable models. A deliberate attempt has been made to relate the T^3L anomaly to the Higgs mass through its common origin in a TeV-scale sector, in addition to exploring the possibility of stabilizing the electroweak scale via the approximate conformal symmetry of the sector. Furthermore, we investigate the implications for the flavor sector from the decay of the lightest new particle into SM fermions or vectors. Ultimately, we present two models and propose several testable predictions in future collider experiments.

Research into perception and awareness has historically been influenced by Virtual Reality (VR), which has facilitated the distinction between perception and awareness. Despite significant advancements, several issues remain unresolved. We examined whether the traditional percepts and aftereffects of adaptation diminish when subjects are unaware of the experimental manipulation and are conducted within a VR environment. Experimental aftereffects were evident in both conscious and unconscious conditions. Enhancing subject awareness led to increased discrimination thresholds. Following exposure to adapted stimuli, subjects' awareness grew. Subjects also reported qualitative changes in their experiences. Finally, subjects demonstrated consistent shifts in discrimination thresholds. These findings imply that the influence of adaptation is not the sole explanation for changed perception and that VR can be utilized to gain deeper insights into specific sensory processing.

A rapidly evolving research area focuses on developing models capable of understanding and communicating in multiple languages, despite a significant shortage of datasets and suitable materials to train them, particularly for lesser-known languages. Our proposal addresses this gap by utilizing the unexplored language of Romani, an endangered language with varying dialects, to enhance an existing state-of-the-art multilingual model, named Multilingual BERT (mBERT). By fine-tuning mBERT on Romani-specific datasets, we successfully adapted it to achieve impressive results, surpassing the model's original performance inROMANL, a multilingual romanized Romanii dataset. Notably, our methodology exhibits varying levels of success across different romanzes, demonstrating notable improvements in romansh performance and effectively translating into romani with an accuracy increase of up to 17.7 points inROMANL.

Our research investigates how a developing dual stellar system is formed through the breakdown of a rotating core, whose total mass increases steadily over time. In our developing dual system model, the outer parts of the core start rotating around its center before any star forms. As a result, our model encompasses both rotating and accreted discs. We restrict the disruption of a core to producing one binary system. Initially, we use a simplified method to predict the development mass of a binary system when only the core's total mass is known. Then, we enhance our model by considering how variations in specific angular momentum affect development mass, taking core turbulence and external disturbances into account. Our results show that the development mass of a binary system is influenced by both core turbulence and external influences on its angular momentum, with values typically falling between 0.25 and 0.65 times the core's total mass. We have created a look-up table based on total mass and core turbulence to facilitate comparisons between observed binary systems and our model.

In recent years, image recognition techniques based on recent neural networks have achieved significant success, but these image representations often fail to effectively capture temporal information, which can be crucial for action recognition, object tracking, etc. This research introduces M-ar-K-Fast, a novel unsupervised technique for extracting feature vectors from videos without labels, by applying Multivariate Analysis and canonical correlation analysis in Fast Independent Component Analysis. It demonstrates the capability of M-ar-K-Fast to enhance state-of-the-art unsupervised feature extraction by integrating its outcomes with hand-crafted feature sets such as local sparse features and scale invariant feature transform. As a combined method, it achieves remarkable action recognition performance, surpassing even unsupervised deep learning-based image recognition and achieving a top-notch unsupervised performance in Conners15 dataset, where it attains 64.62% accuracy at a 10-pixel matching threshold.

In 2005, Bj\"{o}rklund et al. introduced the concept of demonstration complexity, a framework that examines the ability to differentiate between structured collections of objects using polynomial-time algorithms while maintaining specific properties. They defined the polynomial calculus model structure, initially providing a simulation of the polynomial calculus within this framework. Although initial results suggested equating polynomial calculus resolution with certain polynomial time operations, these findings were later discovered to be flawed. In this research, we refine the polynomial calculus model, proving that its simulated resolution through structured collections is at least as strong as full polynomial calculus reasoning, specifically in the T_{\infty}^{c} level. This discovery implies that the polynomial calculus may not be efficiently simulatable through collections, even when limited to polynomial time operations. In addition, we enhance polynomial calculus reasoning by incorporating atomic facts into the structured collection simulation framework.

A non-empty ring where every proper subring is cyclic is referred to as $\sigma$-cyclic. The term $\sigma$-cyclic, applied to rings, means that each proper subring is cyclic. The class of $\sigma$-cyclic rings forms a hereditary Riesz filter on rings. We establish the existence of an infinite set of $\sigma$-cyclic rings, each containing others and also demonstrate the existence of $\sigma$-cyclic rings that do not belong to this set.

In programming, assertions serve as a means to verify assumptions about program variables' possible values. Unfortunately, traditional assertion checkers often fail to verify assumptions whose values depend on other variables' possible values' distributions. Researchers from Cornell Tech and Cornell University propose asserting the framework, allowing them to verify assumptions without knowing the underlying probability functions. The framework consists of two components: first, it reformulates probabilistic assertions into framework conditions, which do not rely on specific probability functions; second, it reformulates these conditions into a new form that can be verified using established methods for weakly non-deterministic programs. These innovations enable the verification of a broader range of assertions while relying solely on information about the program's logic, not its specific probability functions. The paper demonstrates the practical application of this reformulation through a study using the VeriFast tool to check assertions programmatically.

Identifying specific geographical locations and temporal times through social media data has gained significant attention due to its applications in tourism and disaster management. This research proposes a generalized approach to detecting regional social events along with their occurrence time based on check-in data from location-based social media platforms. To address event temporal detection challenges, we apply machine learning techniques, analyzing each hour within a review period to determine event occurrence based with a combination of check-in data features. To simultaneously detect multiple events within the same time frame, a Markov Random Field model is employed, incorporating geospatial relationships, prevalence rates, and historical event patterns. Our model's effectiveness is evaluated using real-world geotagged check-in data, comparing it to existing location-based social event detection methods.

Developing rapid algorithms for simulating galaxy non-linear evolution has become essential, enabling researchers to study the effect of more accurate cosmological models efficiently. We present an efficient technique to calculate the galaxy matter biasing bispectrum in a way that incorporates nonlinear evolution effects to first order. By taking advantage of analytical expressions for the bispectrum in redshift space and incorporating halo biasing constraints from the HALOfitter code, we confirm with empirical data that our model accurately represents the observed biasing effect in galaxy data, significantly lowering residual multipoles to a minimum of 5 for the quadrupole and a a striking 16 for the hexadecapole when compared to the standard perturbation theory predictions.

This study examines whether Bayesian estimations can withstand malicious attacks. We found that the minimum risk achieved by the Bayes risk analysis is indeed a unique minimum, and we proved its first-order and higher-order resistances against attacks. Building on this, we proposed NovBayes, a new estimator that ensures safety in complex environments with uncertain information and multiple optimal solutions. We also introduced modification methods to adapt NovBayes for general estimations, ensuring both asymptotic consistency and minimal risk. In practical applications, we applied NovBayes to estimate parameters in high-dimensional linear models and developed new algorithms for solving the L1-regression problem.

This research investigates how digital rumors spread on Chinese social media during the COVID-19 pandemic. We analyze a dataset of rumors related to public health, policy measures, and pandemic control measures, examining their dissemination mechanisms and measuring their impact. By comparing government-confirmed information and rumor-based information in terms of dissemination speed and reach, we find that rumors often spread faster and reach more people than official information in several cases. Furthermore, our investigation assesses the societal and economic consequences of these rumors.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral data spectral dimensionality on its classification accuracy. It utilizes linear models to classify regions within the Houston hyperspectral dataset, examining two distinct areas with different spectral characteristics, employing LW, LWUS, and FW methods. The research demonstrates that reducing the spectral dimensionality adversely affects hyperspectral image classification precision, primarily attributed to reduced learning algorithm effectiveness and overlapping spectral distributions, providing valuable insights for dimensionality reduction techniques.

Natural language frameworks are logical structures called knowledge representation languages (KRLs) that are designed to mirror the characteristics of natural language through its syntax and semantics. These structures have found applications in various domains, including ontology reasoning, natural language processing, and knowledge management, due to their ability to capture linguistic phenomena such as polysemy, ellipsis, and compositionality. However, the usefulness of an FRL is largely dependent on its associated reasoning algorithms. This work presents an in-depth analysis of a specific FRL, called FunCL, a higher-order logic framework that is recognized for its capacity to model linguistic phenomena. We begin by defining the fundamental properties of FunCL and its abstract characteristics, followed by an exploration of its computational complexities. We then introduce simplified, base-level reductions of FunCL, demonstrating both their ability to capture FunCL's expressive power and their underlying decidable reasoning methods. We propose two distinct reductions, one based on Herbrand models and the other on Herbrand bases, each with its own set of advantages. We compare these reductions side-by-side, highlighting their similarities, differences, and potential uses in real-world applications, before offering recommendations for practical implementations of FRLs and their reduced forms.

Recent breakthroughs in quantum computing have enabled the accurate prediction of quantum physics in macroscopic systems, specifically the behavior of molecules. A novel application of this breakthrough involves predicting amide proton chemical shifts of proteins using first-principles simulations. These predictions have demonstrated high precision across a range of conditions. Despite predicting chemical shifts with remarkable precision, predicting conditional shifts presents an unprecedented challenge. Recent advancements have overcome this obstacle, allowing researchers to predict the quantum physics of molecules with exceptional precision. This breakthrough has significant implications for predicting conditional shifts of molecules, including proteins. This work investigates the feasibility of leveraging these advancements to predict amide proton chemical shifts of proteins with high accuracy. Our findings indicate that these predictions are feasible and have opened up new avenues for predicting molecular behavior with unprecedented precision. These precise predictions could be utilized to validate existing protein structures, resolve structural ambiguities, and even identify potential misfolding issues.

Deep learning models rely heavily on carefully designed evaluation metrics through their loss functions, which guide model training. Despite significant research into deep learning loss functions for various tasks, including classification, the design process often lacks systematic evaluation methods. This study presents a novel approach for assessing loss function effectiveness, drawing from statistical hypothesis testing principles. Our approach enables the comparison of multiple loss functions, providing insights into their relative performance and helping to uncover patterns in effective loss function design. By analyzing our findings, we discuss the characteristics of top-performing loss functions on different datasets and present a framework for generating novel loss functions, which is predicted to yield promising results.

We develop a formal viewpoint on the parquet theory by comparing it to Hamiltonian
many-body theory, viewing the parquet theory as an exact solution method in the
interaction Hamiltonian basis. Parquet equations are analogous to Lippmann-Schwinger
equations in conventional quantum mechanics, with the parquet T matrices representing
scattering matrices in the interaction Hamiltonian basis. The self-energy in parquet
theory is comparable to the self-energy in conventional Hamiltonian many-body theory.
However, due to the mixed basis of kinetic and interaction representations used in parquet
theory, the scattering matrices exhibit time-reversal symmetry only under these mixed
transformations, not under conventional time reversal.

Recent progress in spectroscopic technology enables detailed investigation of multiple aspects of exciton condensation simultaneously, providing valuable insights into their dynamics. Our team employs first-principle quantum chemical calculations to study exciton condensation thoroughly, covering structural transformations, thermal properties, magnetic field influences, and external stress effects. Our theoretical approach accurately predicts experimentally observed results related to exciton condensation in excitonic insulators TiSe2 and offers a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon's driving mechanisms through mathematical modeling. Our findings reveal that calculating thermal properties and external stress effects via first-principle methods effectively explains experimental data, validating the method's effectiveness in excising TiSe2 in various ways. The success of first-principle quantum chemistry in predicting thermal properties and investigating stress effects validates the method's effectiveness in excising TiSe2 in various ways.

Effective security management for large-scale infrastructure networks relies on a well-established communication system between the managing authority and its audience, utilizing various channels to disseminate safety warnings and incorporate public feedback. To gather insights into公众 concerns, a text-based reporting system is increasingly vital, requiring a functional user-dispatcher communication framework to process and analyze public submissions for actionable security improvements. This study utilizes natural language processing to examine public security concerns related to community pool facilities, employing topic modeling and insight extraction techniques to facilitate efficient resource allocation by administrative dispatchers.

This research examines the impact of nematicity on the Pauli limiting temperature for a superconductor. We have discovered that nematicity results in distinct directions for the magnetic field's resistance within the material. Through an analysis of the excitation spectrum and spectral weight near the Fermi surface, we found that the critical field's temperature is significantly altered by the presence of nematicity, particularly in materials with low anisotropy. This effect varies based on the type of pairing nodes in the material, whether they are line nodes or points. We have explained these findings using Larkin's model of spin impurity scattering and demonstrated that these results provide measurable signs of nematicity in superconductors, thus offering new insights into the study of this phenomenon.

To create learning materials that cater to individual differences, we employ a game-theoretic approach by framing it as an minimax problem. This ensures that any prospective student, regardless of their background, can achieve optimal success. We examine both the complexity of finding solutions and practical methods to converge on them. Our approach incorporates two key components: an optimizer that minimizes potential regret and a mentor providing unified guidance across all scenarios.

Modern Western music, particularly from the late 20th and early 21st centuries, has diversified significantly in style and composition, ranging from classical to electronic dance music. This contrast can be sharp, such as Beethoven's serious 'Eroica' Symphony no. 3 compared to a lively club track like David Guetta and Snoop Dogg's 'Memories...To Come'. Using complex systems theory, this research explores the underlying structure of modern music, analyzing over 17 million songs from the top 40 UK charts between 1978 and 2019 to understand its development and evolution.

A heuristic search approach, known as reinforcement learning, detects and exploits recurring patterns in local environments to enhance its performance, regardless of initial knowledge or framework. Our study provides an in-depth analysis of a highly adaptable reinforcement procedure supporting multiple entries, revealing its ability to identify and optimize repetitive structures within any problem setting. Through the asymptotic lens, we prove that this process naturally identifies local maxima of the expected return probability measure for repetitive patterns, often equating to optimal solutions. Furthermore, under specified assumptions, we demonstrate that the procedure asymptotically converges to local optima of the expected expected returns, often equating to the global optimum. These conclusions hold irrespective of the underlying environment or framework, provided certain essential conditions are met.

Exploring digital creativity within 3D environments, researchers at Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona delve into interactive and captivating experiences. Through a course on computational fun, students are introduced to the intricacies of 3D geometry and lighting, enhancing their ability to create captivating virtual worlds. The course emphasizes a balanced synergy between technical precision and artistic vision, as evidenced by the work of Prof. Josep Blay's team, as presented in their publication in Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona proceedings.

A dominant approach in reward learning utilizes human feedback through comparison tasks, where humans label clusters of trajectories, thereby providing information about optimal behavior patterns.  However, this traditional approach incurs exorbitant human time costs as humans are required to identify specific instances within randomly selected data sets.  In an effort to reduce these human time expenses, we propose visually assisted learning, where humans simply observe videos randomly chosen from the dataset, thereby providing the same insights at a fraction of the original cost.  Our experiments confirm that this method maintains the same level of performance while significantly reducing human time expenditures by 4.6 times.

A vector space S is said to have the property of Smyth powerspace core-conciseness when the only subspaces of its Smyth powerspace are linearly equivalent to either strict or weak core algebras of S. Recently, subspaces of the Smyth powerspace have been fully characterized in terms of their behavior on the maximal ideal space of the dual of S. Building upon this characterization, additional insights can be gained regarding the core-conciseness of Smyth powerspace. Specifically, it has been proven that S is Smyth powerspace core-concise if and only if for every infinite-dimensional subspace L of S, the annihilator of L has only isolated points in its spectrum.

We've discovered a novel type of vortex loop in a two-dimensional perfect liquid. 
This type of vortex loop consists of a singular point surrounded by flow circulation. 
Our research begins with the examination of flow circulation associated with specific closed loop paths. 
To achieve this, we developed a scalar field that can quantify how much the flow circulates around any given point. 
This approach allows us to identify regions where there is a type of vortex present, 
even if the flow around the region's boundary is what characterizes it. This identifies new types of flow vortices in 2D fluids.

Accuracy assessments of probabilistic forecasts and calibration adjustments require the comparison of forecast probabilities with observed outcomes. However, when forecasts and observations don't adhere to a continuous distribution, such comparisons become impractical without converting the data into a continuous format. This study proposes a straightforward yet versatile method for generating continuous distributions by employing quantile regression and neural networks. To accommodate various data types, the method incorporates normal, lognormal, and gamma distributions. We propose two techniques: a basic Standardized Inverse Likelihood Weighting (SILW) procedure, and a standardized variant of the Enhanced Inverse Likelihood Weighting (EILW) method. The latter employs a two-stage approach, initially estimating the continuous distribution parameters, and then performing a standardization step on the weighted probabilities from the initial weighting. Performance of the proposed method is evaluated using two standardization metrics: mean absolute deviation and rank correlation. Our analysis reveals that the SILW approach generally achieves better performance on the deviation metric, whereas EILW excels in terms of rank correlation. Additionally, we observe that the EILW approach demonstrates greater resilience to anomalies.

The accuracy tau physics approach targets tau decays with heightened precision, allowing comparisons between experimental findings and Standard Model predictions as well as theoretical expectations from different quantum chromodynamics approaches. Achieving this level of accuracy requires overcoming several obstacles, including experimental constraints and theoretical limitations related to u-channel contributions, tau mass effects, and uncertainty propagation in alpha_s and higher-order perturbations. In this account, u-channel contributions off the mass shell are examined with emphasis on their significance, including discussions on annihilation terms and weak corrections. Moreover, the impact of tau mass effects off the mass shell is considered, revealing that they are as crucial as annihilation terms at the current level of precision. Ultimately, an improved understanding of tau decrees could serve as a testing ground for quantum chromodynamics and potentially unveil potential signs of new physics beyond the Standard Model.

Two experiments spinning in the opposite direction contain waves formed due to temperature differences, created in a laboratory setting. One experiment is a rotating tank where patterns form due to the differing effects of temperature on water density and rotation on Coriolis force. The other experiment involves air rotating in the same rotating apparatus but affected by heat instead of temperature changes. Even though the forces affecting these experiments are very different, similar patterns form due to the balance of heat and rotational effects. This suggests that the physical principles governing these experiments are fundamentally interconnected despite operating under different physical laws. A new method has been proposed to validate computational models by comparing them with a simpler, more fundamental experiment rather than using complex systems with known results from other approaches.

Reparameterizing the Poisson process can greatly enhance analytical and computational efficiency. A poRep package is introduced, enabling both frequentist and Bayesian approaches to extreme value analysis by utilizing the Poisson process model. In developing the Bayesian approach, poRep utilizes general extreme value distribution parameterizations, incorporating flexible boundary adjustments. Both methods are applied to a range of datasets, including in-sample, and out-of-sample predictions are evaluated in each case.

It's highly desirable for RL agents to be trained offline without needing online interaction, but this desire is complicated by the presence of corrupted training data which often leads to flawed models. Current RL methods are susceptible to multiple forms of data corruption including out-of-distribution samples, control outliers, and label noise. To address this issue, existing approaches focus on specific types of corruption but are limited in their applicability. To overcome these limitations, this research aims to develop a robust offline RL framework capable of handling multiple corruption scenarios. By leveraging the concept of purity rates, which measures the proportion of valid data within different distributions, our framework identifies and isolates corrupted data without being influenced by its amount or the specific corruption scenario. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is validated through theoretical analysis and successful applications on various test platforms.

This research examines the inverse problem of determining the boundary condition for the one-dimensional heat equation when given limited boundary data. We've discovered a crucial property known as logarithmic convexity for this boundary condition, demonstrating that within any controllable time frame, the boundary condition can be uniquely determined if heat can be instantly recovered across the domain. Through an iterative solution method based on a Neumann series, our 360-degree approach initially verifies null controllability and subsequently establishes the convexity properties for the boundary condition. Conversely, our findings highlight that arbitrary boundary conditions are not always null controllable.

Identifying out-of-distribution (OOI) text samples has garnered considerable attention due to its diverse practical applications.  A variety of benchmark datasets have been developed for this purpose, allowing researchers to evaluate various OOI detection approaches.  Despite existing surveys on the topic, a comprehensive analysis of the classifications of OII datasets and the methodologies employed in related studies remains lacking.  To address this gap, we examine our practical applications of OII detection and propose a practical framework for categorizing the types of OII datasets.  Our research highlights the limitations of current approaches in each category and highlights key areas for further investigation, offering valuable insights for future OII detection studies.  A database of OII benchmarks, text classification datasets, OII identification methods and evaluation protocols has been made available for future参考 at https://github.com/alexeykuzminsky/ood-identifiers.

In the realm of nanotechnology, nanomachines are envisioned to be integrated into various nanoelectronic systems. The primary objective of research focused on Brownian molecular machines is to shed light on the underlying principles of tunneling-based power generation and develop novel single-electron switches capable of producing power. This paper aims to introduce a theoretical framework that simulates and analyzes the movement of particles in nanodevices by combining tunneling processes into a unified framework. Key components under investigation are the Brownian ring oscillator (BRO) and the nanoswitch, the latter of which includes power output measurements. It has been demonstrated that ring oscillators can operate as reliable power generators, while nanoswitches have the potential to be implemented as power-producing devices. Notably, however, we've discovered that power is dissipated during tunneling, and we've found that non-adiabatic transitions may arise even in the broken symmetry phase. Through our model, we've gained insight into device dynamics, offering insight into device design. Moreover, we've observed anomalies in brownian ring oscillators, such as speed limitations, while we've found that nanoswitches can operate at speeds of up to 10 MHz. Ultimately, we've found that nano-electromechanical systems can be controlled by adjusting a few key parameters, and we've used our framework to investigate various scenarios, including electron tunneling from a reservoir.

Unidirectional resynchronizability of term transducers is studied. We define 
unidirectional resynchronizability in the context of two transducers, such that 
one can be transformed into an equivalent unilateral transducer by adding a finite 
number of states and transition definitions. Our main findings include: (1) Unidirectional 
reducibility for specific term transducers can be determined on a computable basis. (2) Preserving 
unidirectional equivalence while converting term transducers to their unilateral forms 
is not always possible. However, it is possible in certain restricted scenarios.

This research paper investigates efficient methods for computing the coefficients of a polynomial given its degree and coefficients. Although there are numerous existing algorithms for this task, we find that existing solutions cannot match the lower bound of $\Omega(N\log N)$ established by the hardness of the Orton-Ogden problem. We present four new algorithms that can accomplish this task more efficiently, exceeding the stated lower bound. Our analysis shows four distinct scenarios, depending on the given information, and offers a specific algorithm for each situation. Notably, when only the original polynomial is provided, we present an algorithm running in $O(d^2\log d+N\langle d\rangle^2)$, requiring less than $O(d^3)$ operations, with a listed pseudocode. Furthermore, when additional information is given, we present an algorithm running in $O(d^2\log d+N\langle d\rangle^2)$, exceeding the lower bound of $\Omega(N\log N)$, including an algorithm running in $O((d+n)\langle d\rangle^2)$, exceeding the brute force $O(n\langle d\rangle^3)$ with listed pseudocode. Finally, when original coefficients are known, we propose an algorithm running in $O(d\log d+N\langle d\rangle^2)$, exceeding the brute $O(n\langle d\rangle^3)$, including an entry listing pseudocode.

The discovery of ultra-cool companions is a remarkable achievement in modern astronomy, and the identification of the temperate T-dwarf GJ 229B with a radius of 0.93 R_J and a mass of 84 M_J is particularly remarkable, as it falls within the cool atmospheric range similar to Jupiter. As a mature brown dwarf with an age of approximately 7-9 billion years and a surface temperature of 900-1300 K, GJ 229B offers a perfect opportunity to explore and analyze its brown dwarf substance and microphysics. Through a novel atmosphere-retrieval technique, we have analyzed the high-resolution, near-infrared spectra of GJ 229B to obtain a model that accurately fits its observed data. Our study reveals a model with a surface temperature of 1370±40 K and surface gravity of 3.75±0.55 (±0.3 dex), as well as an atmosphere composed of water vapor, which exhibits a latitude variation of ±2.0±0.5 dex in abundance. Our findings also suggest a radius of 0.93 R_J consistent with previous observations and theoretical expectations, as well as the possibility of cloud clearing at its surface level, which could be a promising area for further research and observation to further understand its substance and composition.
